senna.text: Ayrton Senna won three Formula 1 World Championships, in 1988, 1990, and 1991, all with McLaren.
Senna set a career record for pole positions that stood for over a decade after his death.
He died in a crash at the 1994 San Marino Grand Prix at Imola, a weekend that led to sweeping F1 safety reforms.
Senna was famous for his qualifying pace in wet conditions, earning him a reputation as the best wet weather driver of his era.
He and Alain Prost had one of the most intense rivalries in F1 history while teammates at McLaren in 1988 and 1989.

schumacher.text: Michael Schumacher won seven Formula 1 World Championships, a record Lewis Hamilton did not match until 2020.
Five of Schumacher's titles came consecutively with Ferrari from 2000 to 2004.
He won 91 Grand Prix races, a record that stood until Hamilton passed it in 2020.
Schumacher pioneered modern data driven race preparation and physical conditioning in Formula 1.
His son Mick Schumacher also raced in Formula 1, driving for Haas in 2021 and 2022.

monaco-gp.text: The Monaco Grand Prix has been run since 1929, making it one of the oldest races in motorsport.
The circuit is just over 3.3 kilometers, the shortest on the current F1 calendar.
Overtaking is famously difficult at Monaco, qualifying position often decides the race result.
Ayrton Senna won the Monaco Grand Prix six times, a record that still stands.
The race runs through the streets of Monte Carlo, past the harbor where spectators watch from yachts.

hamilton-verstappen-2021.text: The 2021 title fight between Lewis Hamilton and Max Verstappen went to the final lap of the final race.
The season included multiple high profile collisions between the two drivers, including at Silverstone and Monza.
The finale at Abu Dhabi ended in a controversial late safety car call that set up a last lap decider.
Verstappen passed Hamilton on the final lap to win his first World Championship.
The controversy led the FIA to restructure race control procedures for the following season.

ground-effect-2022.text: The 2022 season introduced a major regulation overhaul built around ground effect aerodynamics, the biggest shake up since 1983.
Many cars suffered a violent bouncing phenomenon called porpoising in early 2022, caused by the new floors stalling and reattaching airflow at speed.
The rules were designed to let cars follow more closely by reducing the turbulent wake produced by the car ahead.
Red Bull and Ferrari set the pace under the new rules, with Max Verstappen winning his second title.
The FIA issued mid season technical directives on floor stiffness to address porpoising safety concerns.
